::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 1) you can:

1. **model** a real system as a graph, choosing and defending the type — directed, weighted, bipartite, heterogeneous — as a modeling decision, not a given;
2. **construct and interconvert** the three storage representations — adjacency matrix, adjacency list, edge list (COO) — and state their space costs on sparse graphs;
3. **compute** degrees, the degree matrix, the Laplacian $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$, and walk counts via powers of $\mathbf{A}$, by hand, on small graphs;
4. **classify** any graph problem as node-, edge-, or graph-level and name a deployed industrial instance of each;
5. **explain** why node ordering is storage rather than information, and what that will demand of every model in this course.
:::

## A club splits in two, and a graph sees it coming

In the early 1970s the anthropologist Wayne Zachary spent three years observing a
university karate club — 34 members, and one slow-motion disaster: the instructor
(everyone called him *Mr. Hi*) and the club president (*the Officer*) fell out over
lesson prices, factions formed, and the club tore in half. Every member had to choose a
side.

Zachary had no machine learning — it was 1977. What he had was a record of **who was
friends with whom**: 34 people, 78 friendships. He modeled the split as information
flowing through friendships and predicted each member's choice from the network's
structure alone.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** Out of 34 members, how many do you think structure alone —
no interviews, no attitudes, no demographics, just the friendship graph — predicted
correctly?

::: {.predict-answer}
**33 of 34.** One member (ringed in red below) went against the graph's prediction —
Zachary even explains him: he was weeks from his black-belt exam and could not afford to
leave the instructor, whatever his friendships said. Every failure of a model should
come with a story that good.
:::
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w1-hero.html >}}

That is the thesis of this course, in one 1977 result: **connections carry information
that lives nowhere else.** No column in a spreadsheet about these 34 people — age, rank,
years of membership — predicts the split like the friendships do. The information *is*
the structure.

Half a century later, the systems around you run on the same idea at billion-node scale:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w1-systems.html >}}

This course teaches you to **represent** such data (this week and next), to **learn**
from it (embeddings, then graph neural networks), and to **reason** over it (knowledge
graphs, up to the retrieval systems grounding today's LLMs). Today is the foundation
everything stands on: what a graph is, how a computer holds one, the first numbers you
can squeeze out of pure structure, and the three kinds of questions you can ask.

**Roadmap.** (1) Graphs and their types — a modeling decision. (2) Three ways to store a
graph, and why the honest answer is "the cheap one". (3) First structure numbers:
degrees, walks, and a strange matrix called the Laplacian that will follow us all
semester. (4) The three levels of prediction. (5) A trap involving node ordering that
sets up the deepest idea of the course.

::: {.callout-note title="Recap — what this lecture assumes" collapse="true"}
Only your prerequisites — nothing graph-specific:

- **BFS/DFS** from your algorithms course: how to traverse; we build on the *representations* they used.
- **Matrix multiplication** and what $(\mathbf{M}^2)_{ij} = \sum_k M_{ik}M_{kj}$ unpacks to — one proposition today turns this mechanical fact into a counting device.
- **Big-O** notation for space and time.
- From ML: features live in vectors; models eat tensors. Today's question is how a *relationship* becomes a tensor.
:::

## 1. What is a graph — and which graph?

::: {#def-graph .definition name="Graph"}
A **graph** $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$ is a set of **nodes**
$\mathcal{V}$ and a set of **edges** $\mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{V} \times \mathcal{V}$,
each edge a pair of nodes. A **simple graph** is undirected, with no self-loops and at
most one edge per pair; $n = |\mathcal{V}|$, $m = |\mathcal{E}|$. Each node $u$ may
carry a **feature vector** $\mathbf{x}_u \in \mathbb{R}^{m_0}$, stacked into
$\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m_0}$.
:::

::: {.math-note}
Nodes are the entities, edges are the relationships, features are what a spreadsheet
would have told you anyway. The whole course lives in the tension between
$\mathbf{X}$ (what things are) and $\mathcal{E}$ (how things relate).
:::

Meet the graph that will star on our whiteboard for all fifteen weeks — six nodes, each
with its own permanent color, so that in any later diagram you can follow an individual
node through a construction:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-input-graph.html >}}

The definition above is the *plainest* graph. Real systems usually need more, and the
choice of *which* graph to build is a genuine modeling decision — arguably the most
consequential one you will make in any graph project:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w1-types.html >}}

Names to keep: **directed** graphs when the relation is one-way (citations, follows,
web links — a citation *from* a survey means something different than one *to* it);
**weighted** when the relation has magnitude; **bipartite** when nodes come in two sets
and edges only cross between them (users×items — the entire recommender-systems industry
lives on this shape, Week 14); **heterogeneous** when nodes and edges carry *types* —
the shape of a <span class="term" data-def="Knowledge graph: a heterogeneous graph whose typed edges are read as facts — (head entity, relation, tail entity) triples, like (Innopolis University, located_in, Tatarstan). Weeks 4–5 are devoted to them.">knowledge graph</span>,
which we treat as a first-class citizen of this course starting Week 4; **multigraphs**
when a pair can be connected more than once (two transactions between the same
accounts).

One modeling honesty note before moving on: sometimes there is no graph until *you*
build one — practitioners routinely create k-nearest-neighbor graphs over plain
vectors, co-occurrence graphs over text, correlation graphs over time series. The graph
is then a lens you chose, and every conclusion downstream inherits that choice. We will
return to this in the pitfalls.

## 2. Handing a graph to a computer

A graph is a set of pairs — sets are not tensors, and your GPU eats tensors. There are
exactly three standard ways to serialize the relationship structure, and you should be
able to write all three from memory:

::: {#def-adj .definition name="Adjacency matrix"}
The **adjacency matrix** of a graph on nodes $1..n$ is
$\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ with $\mathbf{A}[u,v] = 1$ if
$(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}$ and $0$ otherwise — real-valued for weighted graphs, symmetric
exactly when the graph is undirected, and generally *not* symmetric for directed ones.
:::

The **adjacency list** stores, per node, the list of its neighbors — the representation
your BFS used. The **edge list** just stores the $m$ pairs; stacked as a $2 \times m$
integer tensor it is called
<span class="term" data-def="COO — coordinate format: a sparse tensor stored as the list of coordinates of its nonzero entries. A graph's edge list IS its adjacency matrix in COO form. PyTorch Geometric's edge_index is exactly this.">COO format</span>,
and under the name `edge_index` it is the representation PyTorch Geometric — and
therefore this course's labs — runs on.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w1-representations.html >}}

Build the intuition with your hands — edit the graph and watch every representation
track it:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w1-builder.html >}}

### Which one, then? Follow the money

::: {#prp-storage .proposition name="Storage costs"}
For a graph with $n$ nodes and $m$ undirected edges, the adjacency matrix stores
$n^2$ entries regardless of $m$; the adjacency list stores $n + 2m$; the edge list
$2m$. For a **sparse** graph — $m = O(n)$, the regime of essentially every real
network — the matrix is a factor $\Theta(n)$ more expensive than either alternative.
:::

::: {.math-note}
The matrix buys $O(1)$ edge lookup and the ability to *multiply* (next section); the
lists buy survival. Real systems store lists/COO and materialize matrix *products*
without ever materializing the matrix — you will meet this trick as "sparse matmul" in
Week 6 and live inside it from then on.
:::

Real graphs are dramatically sparse: Cora averages under 4 citations per paper;
ogbn-products, with 2.4 million products, averages ~50 co-purchases — meaning its
adjacency matrix would be **99.998% zeros**. Feel the scaling yourself:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w1-cost.html >}}

## 3. First numbers from pure structure

Before any learning, the representations themselves already answer questions. Three
objects, all built from $\mathbf{A}$, will follow us to Week 15.

**Degree.** $d_u = \sum_v \mathbf{A}[u,v]$ — how connected a node is; collected into the
diagonal **degree matrix** $\mathbf{D}$. In the karate club, Mr. Hi and the Officer are
the two highest-degree nodes — the hubs the factions formed around. (Degree is the first
and crudest of the *centralities*; Week 2 builds the full toolbox.)

**Walks, by matrix power.** Here is the first genuinely surprising payoff of the matrix
representation:

::: {#prp-walks .proposition name="Powers of A count walks"}
For any $k \ge 1$, $(\mathbf{A}^k)[u,v]$ equals the number of **walks** of length
exactly $k$ from $u$ to $v$ (a walk may revisit nodes and edges). In particular
$(\mathbf{A}^2)[u,u] = d_u$, and for $u \neq v$, $(\mathbf{A}^2)[u,v]$ counts the
**common neighbors** of $u$ and $v$.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (induction on k — worth doing once in your life)</summary>
Base case $k = 1$: $\mathbf{A}[u,v]$ is $1$ exactly when a length-1 walk (an edge)
exists, and a pair has at most one. Inductive step: assume $(\mathbf{A}^{k-1})[u,w]$
counts length-$(k{-}1)$ walks $u \to w$. Every length-$k$ walk $u \to v$ is a
length-$(k{-}1)$ walk to some neighbor $w$ of $v$, followed by the edge $(w,v)$, and
this decomposition is unique. Summing over the possible penultimate nodes:
$\#\{\text{length-}k\text{ walks } u \to v\} = \sum_w (\mathbf{A}^{k-1})[u,w] \, \mathbf{A}[w,v] = (\mathbf{A}^k)[u,v]$
— which is precisely the definition of the matrix product. $\square$
</details>

::: {#exm-walks .example name="Hand computation on the cast graph"}
On the cast graph (edges $AB, AC, AD, BC, CE, CF, EF$): $(\mathbf{A}^2)[A,A] = d_A = 3$.
$(\mathbf{A}^2)[A,C]$ counts common neighbors of $A$ and $C$: their neighbor sets are
$\{B, C, D\}$ and $\{A, B, E, F\}$, sharing only $B$ — so $1$: the single 2-walk
$A \to B \to C$. And $(\mathbf{A}^2)[A,F]$? Common neighbors of $A$ and $F$: $\{B,C,D\} \cap \{C,E\} = \{C\}$ — again $1$,
the walk $A \to C \to F$. You will verify all 36 entries with one line of code in the
lab; on the midterm you may be asked for two or three of them with a pencil.
:::

Common-neighbor counts are not a toy: "how many mutual friends" is the baseline behind
every "people you may know" feature, and in Week 3 it becomes the first serious
link-prediction heuristic.

**The Laplacian.** The strangest and most durable object of the week:

::: {#def-lap .definition name="Graph Laplacian"}
$\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$: degrees on the diagonal, $-1$ for each edge off
it. Every row sums to zero.
:::

::: {#prp-lap .proposition name="The Laplacian is a variation meter"}
For any signal $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ (one number per node),

$$
\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L} \mathbf{x} \;=\; \sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}} (x_u - x_v)^2 .
$$

The quadratic form measures how much $\mathbf{x}$ **disagrees across edges** — zero
exactly when $\mathbf{x}$ is constant on every connected component, large when
neighbors differ.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (expand and regroup)</summary>
$\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{D} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}
= \sum_u d_u x_u^2 - \sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}} 2 x_u x_v$.
In the first term, each edge $(u,v)$ contributes $x_u^2$ once (via $d_u$) and $x_v^2$
once (via $d_v$); so both sums range over edges:
$\sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}} (x_u^2 + x_v^2 - 2x_u x_v) = \sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}} (x_u - x_v)^2$. $\square$
</details>

Why care, this week? Because "how much does a quantity vary across edges" is the
mathematical form of the question the karate club answered: allegiance varied *little*
across friendships — friends chose the same side. That tendency has a name you will use
weekly, <span class="term" data-def="Homophily: connected nodes tend to be alike — friends share sides, papers cite their own topic, fraudsters transact with mules. The single assumption doing the most silent work in graph ML; its failure (heterophily) is where naive methods break.">**homophily**</span>,
and the Laplacian is the instrument that measures it. Next week $\mathbf{L}$ finds
communities; in Week 6 its eigenvectors become the *frequencies* of a graph and explain
what "convolutional" means in GCN. When a matrix keeps showing up like that, learn its
face early.

## 4. Three levels of asking

Every graph-ML product you will ever build answers a question at one of exactly three
levels, and the level dictates the loss, the data splits, and the metrics — get the
level wrong and nothing downstream can save you.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w1-tasks.html >}}

Anchor each level to a system that pays salaries: **node-level** — integrity scoring at
every large platform (is this account a bot?), paper topics on Cora (our Week 6
running example); **edge-level** — "people you may know", product recommendation, and
knowledge-graph completion (which missing fact is true? — Weeks 4–5); **graph-level** —
molecular property prediction (the screen that surfaced the antibiotic halicin ran a
graph-level model over millions of candidate molecules), malware detection on call
graphs.

Semi-supervised framing, which will be our default: in the karate club, imagine you
observed the choices of only *four* members and had to fill in the other thirty from
the friendship structure. That — few labels, full structure — is exactly the setting of
Cora and of Week 6.

## 5. The ordering trap

One more foundation stone, disguised as a bookkeeping remark. To write $\mathbf{A}$ at
all, we had to *number* the nodes — the cast graph's matrix came out as it did because
we chose $A{=}1, \dots, F{=}6$. Nothing in the club or the citation network chose that
numbering; storage did.

::: {.predict}
**Predict.** Our six-node cast graph can be numbered $6! = 720$ different ways, giving
up to 720 different adjacency matrices for the *same* graph. Suppose you feed two of
those matrices, flattened into vectors, to an ordinary MLP. Same graph in both cases —
does the MLP give the same answer?

::: {.predict-answer}
**No — in general it gives 720 different answers to one question.** The MLP reads
positions, positions encode our arbitrary numbering, so it learns storage artifacts.
Fixing this properly — building models whose answers provably cannot depend on the
numbering — is called *permutation invariance*, it is the deepest idea in this course,
and in Week 6 we will prove our models have it and catch an MLP failing it, live. For
now, carry the warning: **node order is storage, not information.**
:::
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 1 · Reaching for the dense matrix because the formula has an A in it" icon="false"}
Formulas are written with $\mathbf{A}$; code should almost never materialize it. At
$n = 10^6$ — a small industrial graph — dense $\mathbf{A}$ is 4 TB. The formula's
$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ is computed from the edge list in $O(m)$. Translate math to
sparse ops reflexively; Lab 1 starts the habit.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 2 · Symmetrizing a directed relation without noticing" icon="false"}
Loading citations, follows, or web links into an undirected structure silently asserts
"X cites Y" ≡ "Y cites X" — destroying, for citation networks, the entire notion of
influence direction. Libraries do this *for* you if you use the wrong loader flag. Know
which of your relations are truly symmetric; it is a modeling claim, not a default.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 3 · “The graph is given”" icon="false"}
Someone chose those edges — a logging pipeline, a thresholded similarity, a k-NN
builder, a business rule. Different choice, different graph, different conclusions.
Interrogate the edge definition of any dataset before trusting results on it; when
*you* build the graph, report the recipe as part of the model.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 4 · Judging a graph by its hairball" icon="false"}
Force-directed drawings of more than a few hundred nodes are decoration, not analysis —
layout algorithms invent geometry that is not in the data. Judge graphs by statistics
(degrees, components, clustering — Week 2) and by task performance; draw only what is
small enough to read, as our figures do.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 5 · Assuming your graph behaves like the karate club" icon="false"}
Today's success story ran on homophily: friends chose alike. Transaction graphs,
dating graphs, and protein interactions routinely violate it — connected nodes
*differ* systematically. Every structure-based method you will learn makes an
assumption of this kind somewhere; the professional habit is to check it (Week 2 gives
you the tools) before believing any result.
:::

## In this week's lab

[Lab 1](../labs/lab01.qmd) is the course onboarding: you set up the exact Colab + PyTorch
Geometric environment used all semester, load the real karate club and reproduce today's
hero figure's data, build the cast graph as a PyG `edge_index` **by hand** (and check it
against assertions), compute degrees, $\mathbf{A}^2$, and the Laplacian in torch —
verifying @exm-walks numerically — and take a first look at Cora, the dataset that

graphs are concrete objects before Week 4 formalizes them.

## Required reading

**1 · Battaglia et al. — *Relational inductive biases, deep learning, and graph networks* (2018).** [arXiv:1806.01261](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.01261)

::: {.reading-annotation}
The position paper for the whole field: deep learning wins when architecture matches
data structure, and graphs are the most general structure. Read Sections 1–2 closely —
Table 1, mapping fully-connected/convolutional/recurrent layers to their relational
assumptions, is the single most important artifact; skim the graph-network formalism in
Section 3 on first pass (it returns in Week 6). There are no experiments — that is the
point: read it for the argument.
:::

**2 · Hamilton, Ying & Leskovec — *Representation Learning on Graphs: Methods and Applications* (IEEE DEB 2017).** [arXiv:1709.05584](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.05584)

::: {.reading-annotation}
The survey whose framing organizes this course: every method is an encoder + a decoder +
a similarity + a loss. Internalize that four-part template from Section 2 — it is the
mental filing cabinet you will slot DeepWalk, TransE, and GCNs into over the coming
weeks. Notice how today's task taxonomy becomes downstream uses of embeddings. Skip the
architecture details for now; we return to each in depth.
:::

**Also see:** Hamilton, *GRL book*, §1.1–1.2 (definitions and tasks — our notation
follows it) · CS224W lecture "Introduction".

**Optional:** Sanchez-Lengeling et al., [A Gentle Introduction to Graph Neural
Networks](https://doi.org/10.23915/distill.00033) (Distill 2021) — the interactive
article this course's style descends from; play with its widgets ·
Derrow-Pinion et al., [ETA Prediction with GNNs in Google Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.11482)
(CIKM 2021) — today's road-network panel, deployed for a billion users ·
Ying et al., [PinSage](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.01973) (KDD 2018) — the
bipartite-graph shape at Pinterest scale; read the systems story, defer the math.

## Check your understanding

<details><summary>Q1 · Modeling — A dataset of bank transfers: accounts, transfers with amounts and timestamps, some accounts flagged as mules. Choose the graph type and justify each property you keep.</summary>
Directed (money flows one way — symmetrizing destroys the laundering pattern),
weighted (amounts matter), multigraph or timestamped edges (repeat transfers between
the same pair are the signal, not noise), homogeneous nodes but with features
(account age, KYC status). The task is node-level (flag mules) — and note this graph is
likely *heterophilous*: mules transact with victims, not with other mules (Pitfall 5).
</details>

<details><summary>Q2 · Hand computation — On the cast graph, compute (A²)[B,F] and name the walks it counts. Then explain why (A²)[u,u] = dᵤ in one sentence.</summary>
Neighbors of $B$: $\{A, C\}$; neighbors of $F$: $\{C, E\}$; common: $\{C\}$ — so
$(\mathbf{A}^2)[B,F] = 1$, the walk $B \to C \to F$. Diagonal: a length-2 walk from $u$
back to $u$ must go out along one of $u$'s $d_u$ edges and immediately return along the
same edge, giving exactly $d_u$ such walks.
</details>

<details><summary>Q3 · Representations — Your graph has n = 10⁷ nodes and m = 5·10⁷ edges. Give the entry counts for all three representations and say which you would use for (a) repeated "are u,v connected?" queries, (b) feeding a PyG model, (c) a whiteboard derivation.</summary>
Dense matrix: $n^2 = 10^{14}$ entries (≈ 400 TB at 4 B — nonexistent). Adjacency list:
$n + 2m = 1.1 \times 10^8$. Edge list: $2m = 10^8$. For (a) neither raw list is ideal —
a hash set of edges or sorted adjacency (binary search) gives fast membership; (b) COO
`edge_index`; (c) the dense matrix — on the whiteboard, $n = 6$ and clarity wins. The
representation is a tool choice per operation, not an identity.
</details>

<details><summary>Q4 · Laplacian — Compute row A of L for the cast graph, and evaluate xᵀLx for x = (1,1,1,1,0,0) (nodes A..F). What is the quadratic form counting here?</summary>
$d_A = 3$, $A$'s neighbors are $B, C, D$: row $A$ of $\mathbf{L}$ is
$(3, -1, -1, -1, 0, 0)$. The form sums $(x_u - x_v)^2$ over edges; $x$ is the indicator
of $\{A,B,C,D\}$, so only edges crossing to $\{E,F\}$ contribute $1$ each: edges $CE$
and $CF$ — total $\mathbf{2}$. The quadratic form counts the **cut edges** of the
partition — precisely the quantity next week's community detection minimizes.
</details>

<details><summary>Q5 · Tasks — Classify each as node-, edge-, or graph-level: (a) will this user churn?, (b) is this new molecule soluble?, (c) how long will this road segment take at 6pm?, (d) which paper should this citation-manager suggest next?</summary>
(a) node-level; (b) graph-level; (c) edge-level (the segment is an edge of the road
graph — Google Maps' actual setup); (d) edge-level (link prediction between user/paper
or paper/paper). If you hesitated on (c): what is a node and what is an edge is itself
a modeling decision — road intersections as nodes makes segments edges.
</details>

<details><summary>Q6 · The trap — Your colleague trains a fraud model that takes the first 100 rows of the adjacency matrix as features "because the important accounts come first". Give two distinct reasons this is broken.</summary>
(1) Ordering is storage: renumber the accounts and the model's inputs — and answers —
change for the identical graph; "comes first" is an artifact of the export script.
(2) Even granting a meaningful order, row $u$ of $\mathbf{A}$ is an $n$-dimensional
one-hot-neighborhood vector: it cannot transfer to graphs of other sizes and treats
"connected to account #37" as a feature — memorization, not structure. Both failures
are cured by the permutation-invariant machinery this course builds.
</details>

<details><summary>Q7 · Transfer — Zachary's model predicted the split from structure. State the assumption that made this possible, and describe a real network where the same method would fail badly.</summary>
Homophily: allegiance varied smoothly across friendships (small $\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}$
for the allegiance signal). A heterophilous counterexample: a bipartite
fraudster–victim transaction network — connected nodes are systematically *opposite*,
so "predict my label from my neighbors' labels" inverts the truth. Checking which
regime you are in, before modeling, is the Week 2 skill.
</details>

## Where this leaves us

You can now put a real system into a graph, store it honestly, and read off its first
numbers. What you cannot yet do is *rank* — which node matters most, which two nodes
belong to the same community, whether this graph is even the homophilous kind our
methods will assume. Structure has much more to say before any learning happens:
centralities that found search engines, a relabeling trick from 1968 that will turn out
to bound what neural networks can ever see on a graph, and the community-finding
machinery that Zachary's little club launched. That is Week 2: **classical graph ML —
structure as features.** Bring the Laplacian; it works there too.

:::
